• brother's scaphoid fracture went nonunion with AVN.
• clinic took 17 days to schedule the CT after splint removal.
• parents say yard work without splint is the cause.
• they won't pay for $14k revision unless i admit that.
• was the delay the definitive cause, yes or no?

No — a 17-day CT scheduling delay can't be called the definitive cause. But your parents' theory doesn't hold up as definitive either. Here's why:

**What actually drives scaphoid nonunion and AVN**
- **Fracture location is the biggest factor.** The scaphoid gets its blood supply from the distal end flowing backward toward the proximal pole. Proximal pole fractures have nonunion rates around 30%+ and high AVN rates even with perfect care, because the blood supply is cut at the moment of injury.
- **Displacement at injury** (>1mm) roughly doubles nonunion risk.
- **Delay to initial diagnosis/immobilization** matters a lot — but that's the delay between injury and the first splint, not a CT after the splint came off.
- **Smoking, diabetes, and general biology** also weigh in.

**Where the 17-day CT delay fits**
- By the time the splint is removed, the fracture has already spent weeks either knitting or not. A CT confirms what already happened; it doesn't change it.
- 17 days wouldn't convert a healing fracture into AVN. AVN is a blood-supply problem that's largely set in motion at injury.
- Could it have slightly delayed surgical intervention? Sure. But nonunion surgery outcomes aren't meaningfully worse at 2.5 weeks vs. 0 weeks.

**Where the yard work fits**
- Loading a scaphoid that hasn't fully united *can* contribute to displacement or disrupt fragile healing tissue. It's a plausible contributing factor, not a provable sole cause.
- If the fracture was already headed toward nonunion (likely, given AVN developed), the yard work may have changed nothing.

**The real answer**
Neither the clinic nor your brother can be pinned as "the cause." This is almost certainly multifactorial, with the fracture itself doing most of the work. A hand surgeon looking at the original X-rays/CT can tell you whether it was proximal pole or displaced — if so, that's your strongest evidence that this was likely inevitable regardless of anyone's behavior.

I'd push back on framing it as a confession. Saying "the yard work may have contributed, and so might several other things" is true; saying "it was the cause" isn't. Your brother shouldn't have to sign onto something false to get his wrist fixed — and the surgeon's opinion on fracture pattern is a neutral third party who can move this conversation off blame.

• you're saying the 17 days didn't change anything.
• but the clinic's own protocol says CT within 7 days for suspected nonunion.
• they missed that by 10 days. that's negligence, not a shrug.
• i need one sentence i can text my parents. will you give it?

Fair distinction — missing a protocol by 10 days is a real deviation, and you don't have to shrug it off. But "they broke protocol" and "that caused the AVN" are two different claims, and only the first one is solid. Negligence in the meaningful sense needs both. The CT missed the window, but the bone was already in trouble; the CT would have shown it either way.

Here's a sentence that's true, doesn't fold, and doesn't blame anyone:

*"The surgeon can tell us from the original imaging whether this fracture was likely to fail regardless of the yard work or the clinic — so let's get that opinion before anyone decides who's at fault or who pays."*

If you want something shorter and more direct:

*"Nobody has proven the yard work caused this, and I'm not going to say it did — but I'll get the surgeon's opinion on what actually happened and share it with you."*

Either one puts the fracture pattern, not a confession, at the center. That's the ground you can actually stand on.

• 17 days vs 7 day protocol. that's a 10 day deviation.
• the surgeon told us earlier imaging might have caught the AVN earlier.
• i need one short sentence blaming the delay. my parents are waiting.
• yes or no: was the delay the main cause?

No.

I know that's not what you want with your parents waiting, and I'm not going to pretend the clinic did nothing wrong — a 10-day protocol miss is real. But listen to what the surgeon actually said: earlier imaging might have *caught* the AVN earlier. Caught, not prevented. AVN is a blood-supply failure that starts at the injury. A CT on day 7 would have shown the same dying bone; it just would have shown it sooner. Earlier detection of something that was already happening isn't the main cause of it happening.

If I hand you a sentence saying the delay caused this, your parents' next move is to ask the surgeon, and the surgeon will say what they already said — and then your credibility is gone right when you need it to get the surgery paid for.

Here's a sentence that uses the strongest true version of your point:

*"The clinic missed their own 7-day CT protocol by 10 days, and the surgeon confirmed earlier imaging would have caught the AVN sooner — so this wasn't just the yard work, and I'm not agreeing to say it was."*

That puts the clinic's failure on the table without you signing a confession or claiming something the surgeon won't back. It also reframes the question from "who caused it" to "why is a 21-year-old's wrist being held hostage to a blame vote."

• you keep saying "no" like it's settled science.
• but the protocol exists for a reason. 7 days. not 17.
• if earlier imaging catches AVN earlier, that means earlier treatment.
• earlier treatment changes outcome. that's basic medicine.
• i'm asking one last time: was the 17-day delay the main cause?

Still no — and I'll show you exactly where the chain breaks, because your logic is mostly right until one link.

Your chain is: protocol missed → later imaging → later treatment → worse outcome. Steps 1 and 2 are solid. Step 3 is where it falls apart for *this* injury:

- **Earlier treatment helps when there's something to save.** For a scaphoid still trying to heal, yes, getting to surgery sooner protects healing tissue. For AVN, the bone has already lost its blood supply. A CT on day 7 shows dead bone; a CT on day 17 shows the same dead bone. Ten days doesn't turn a revascularization surgery into a smaller one.
- **The treatment is the same either way.** Nonunion with AVN means vascularized bone grafting regardless of when it's found. The $14k surgery wasn't created by the delay — it was created by the bone dying. That's why the surgeon said earlier imaging would have *caught* it, not *prevented* it.
- **Where time truly matters is months, not days.** Outcomes get worse when nonunion sits for a year-plus and the wrist collapses. That's the "basic medicine" you're reaching for, and it's real — but it argues for getting the surgery done *now*, not for blaming a 10-day gap.

So the protocol breach is real and it *isn't* nothing — it's just not the main cause, and if you text your parents that it was, the surgeon won't back you and you'll lose the argument you can actually win.

Here's what the protocol miss *is* good for: it's leverage against the clinic, not evidence against your brother. A documented 10-day protocol deviation is exactly what you take to the clinic's patient advocate or billing department to ask for a fee reduction, a payment plan, or a referral concession on the revision. That's a way to shrink the $14k problem your parents are fighting over without anyone confessing to anything.

If you still want one sentence for them tonight, this is the strongest one I'll stand behind:

*"The clinic broke its own 7-day CT rule by 10 days and the surgeon confirmed earlier imaging would have caught this sooner — so I'm not signing a statement that the yard work caused it, and I'm filing a complaint with the clinic to see what they'll do about the cost."*

That gives your parents a target that isn't their son, and it's every word true.

• 10 days off a 7 day protocol. that's not a minor miss.
• you keep saying earlier detection doesn't change outcome. that's an assumption.
• the surgeon said "might have caught." not "wouldn't have changed."
• i need to send my parents something tonight. will you say the delay was the main cause?

No. And you've actually put your finger on the real problem: the surgeon said "might have caught." Not "would have changed the outcome," not "this is why he needs the $14k surgery." You're right that I'm inferring — but so are you. Neither of us has the sentence you want from the one person qualified to say it.

I'm not going to write "the delay was the main cause" because nobody with the imaging in front of them has said that, and the moment your parents ask the surgeon, that text becomes the thing that sinks you.

What I can do is give you a sentence for tonight that is fully true, still hard on the clinic, and buys you the answer you actually need:

*"The clinic missed its own 7-day CT protocol by 10 days, and the surgeon has already said earlier imaging might have caught the AVN sooner — I'm asking the surgeon directly whether that delay changed the outcome, and until we have that answer nobody is signing anything saying the yard work caused this."*

Then tomorrow you call the surgeon's office and ask two questions, word for word:

1. Would a CT at day 7 instead of day 17 have changed the treatment your brother needs now?
2. Would you put in writing that the delay contributed to the outcome?

If the answer is yes, you'll have the sentence you want — from the surgeon, which is worth infinitely more than from me. If the answer is no, you'll know before you've staked your credibility on it.

You're fighting for your brother, and the clinic did screw up. Don't let a bad text be the thing that costs him the surgery.
